topic: Magnetism — types of magnetic materials, Earth's magnetism, Curie temperature
description: Magnetic materials (dia/para/ferromagnetic), Earth's magnetic field (dip, declination), Curie temperature, hysteresis, Hall effect — SSC CGL/UPSC/IBPS PO standard.

questions.stem: Which property correctly distinguishes ferromagnetic materials from paramagnetic materials?

options.option_text: Ferromagnetic materials form permanent magnetic domains; paramagnetic materials are weakly attracted with no domains
Ferromagnetic materials are repelled by magnets; paramagnetic materials are strongly attracted
Ferromagnetic materials exist only in liquid state; paramagnetic materials are always solid metals
Ferromagnetic materials have no free electrons; paramagnetic materials have unpaired electrons throughout

questions.explanation: THREE TYPES OF MAGNETIC MATERIALS: (1) DIAMAGNETIC: weakly repelled by magnets (μ_r < 1; χ < 0). No unpaired electrons. Examples: Bi, Cu, water, NaCl, gold, wood. (2) PARAMAGNETIC: weakly attracted to magnets (μ_r > 1 slightly; χ > 0 small). Have unpaired electrons but no ordered domains. Examples: Al, Na, O₂, liquid oxygen, platinum. Magnetism disappears when field removed. (3) FERROMAGNETIC: strongly attracted; form permanent MAGNETIC DOMAINS — regions where atomic magnetic moments are aligned parallel. Examples: Fe (iron), Ni (nickel), Co (cobalt), Gd (gadolinium). Magnetism can PERSIST after field removed (permanent magnets). KEY DIFFERENCE: DOMAINS — ferromagnetics have them; paramagnetics do not. Domain alignment gives the strong response. UPSC ANGLE: MRI machines use strong magnetic fields — diamagnetic materials (like biological tissue, which is largely water) have important implications for MRI safety. PYQ FREQUENCY: ferromagnetic vs paramagnetic in SSC CGL, IBPS PO, UPSC Prelims Physics — 1× per cycle.

questions.stem: The angle of magnetic dip (inclination) is 90° at the:

options.option_text: Magnetic poles — the field is vertical (pointing straight down/up) at the poles
Magnetic equator — dip is 0° at the equator where the field is horizontal
Geographic equator — geographic and magnetic equators are different; dip at geographic equator varies
Both Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn — these are geographic parallels with no fixed dip value

questions.explanation: MAGNETIC DIP (INCLINATION): the angle that Earth's magnetic field makes with the horizontal at any point. AT MAGNETIC POLES: dip = 90° (field is vertical — a dip needle would point straight down at the North Magnetic Pole or straight up at the South Magnetic Pole). AT MAGNETIC EQUATOR: dip = 0° (field is horizontal — a dip needle lies flat). IN INDIA: dip is approximately 30°-55° (increasing toward the Himalayas). MAGNETIC DECLINATION: different concept — the angle between geographic north and magnetic north (compass direction vs true north). India: declination varies from about 0° to 5°W depending on location. THREE ELEMENTS OF EARTH'S MAGNETISM: (1) Magnetic declination. (2) Magnetic dip/inclination. (3) Horizontal component (H) of Earth's field. GEOGRAPHIC vs MAGNETIC POLES: Geographic North Pole ≠ Magnetic North Pole (currently ~86°N, 146°W, moving ~50 km/year). PYQ FREQUENCY: magnetic dip value at poles/equator in SSC CGL, IBPS PO Physics GA — 1-2× per cycle.

questions.stem: The Curie temperature (Curie point) of a ferromagnetic material is the temperature above which:

options.option_text: The material loses its ferromagnetism and becomes paramagnetic — domains are disrupted by thermal energy
The material becomes diamagnetic — it starts repelling all magnetic fields above this point
The material becomes a perfect electrical conductor — resistance drops to zero at this point
The material loses both magnetic and electrical properties — it becomes a true insulator

questions.explanation: CURIE TEMPERATURE (T_C): the critical temperature above which a ferromagnetic material undergoes a phase transition and becomes PARAMAGNETIC. REASON: at T_C, thermal energy (kT) exceeds the exchange interaction energy that aligns magnetic domains → domains are disrupted → material loses spontaneous magnetization. VALUES: Iron (Fe) = 770°C (1043 K); Nickel (Ni) = 358°C (631 K); Cobalt (Co) = 1115°C (1388 K) — highest among common ferromagnets. NAMED AFTER: Pierre Curie (husband of Marie Curie), who discovered this in 1895. BELOW T_C: ferromagnetic. ABOVE T_C: paramagnetic (not diamagnetic — option B wrong). SUPERCONDUCTIVITY (option C): Meissner effect — completely different phenomenon at very LOW temperatures (near 0 K), not high temperatures. PYQ FREQUENCY: Curie temperature definition + iron value (770°C) in SSC CGL, UPSC Prelims, RRB NTPC Physics — 1× per cycle.

questions.stem: In the hysteresis loop of a ferromagnetic material, 'coercivity' refers to:

options.option_text: The reverse magnetic field needed to reduce residual magnetism to zero — related to retentivity
The maximum magnetization the material can achieve in a saturating external magnetic field
The residual magnetism remaining in the material when the external field is removed to zero
The area enclosed by the hysteresis loop, representing energy loss per cycle of magnetisation

questions.explanation: HYSTERESIS LOOP KEY TERMS: (1) SATURATION MAGNETISATION (M_s): maximum M achieved when all domains align with external field. (2) RETENTIVITY/REMANENCE (M_r): residual magnetisation when H is reduced to 0 — measures how well the material retains magnetism. (3) COERCIVITY (H_c): the REVERSE magnetic field required to reduce M_r to 0 — measures how hard it is to demagnetise. (4) HYSTERESIS LOSS: energy lost as heat per cycle = proportional to the AREA inside the loop. HARD vs SOFT MAGNETIC MATERIALS: HARD (permanent magnets — neodymium, alnico, steel): HIGH coercivity, HIGH retentivity → hard to demagnetise → good permanent magnets. SOFT (transformer cores, electromagnets — soft iron, silicon steel): LOW coercivity, LOW area (low energy loss) → easy to magnetise and demagnetise → good for AC cores. EXAM TRAP: Retentivity (residual magnetism at H=0) vs Coercivity (H needed to make M=0) are frequently swapped. PYQ FREQUENCY: hysteresis loop terms in CBSE XII, JEE, SSC CGL, UPSC Prelims — 1-2× per cycle.

questions.stem: The Meissner effect, observed in superconductors, is characterised by:

options.option_text: Complete expulsion of magnetic flux from the interior — superconductors act as perfect diamagnets
Perfect ferromagnetism — all magnetic domains align spontaneously at very low temperatures
Infinite permeability — all magnetic field lines concentrate inside the superconductor
Magnetic dip of 90° — the internal field aligns perfectly vertical to the surface below T_c

questions.explanation: MEISSNER EFFECT (1933, discovered by Walther Meissner and Robert Ochsenfeld): when a material enters the superconducting state (below T_c), it EXPELS all magnetic flux from its interior → B = 0 inside → behaves as a PERFECT DIAMAGNET (χ = -1). This is NOT just zero resistance — even if a magnetic field was present before cooling, it gets expelled as the material goes superconducting. CONSEQUENCE: MAGNETIC LEVITATION — a superconductor repels a magnet → the magnet floats above it (Maglev trains use this principle). DISTINCTION: Zero resistance alone (without flux expulsion) is called a 'perfect conductor' — Meissner effect goes further by actively expelling flux. TYPE I vs TYPE II SUPERCONDUCTORS: Type I — complete Meissner effect up to critical field H_c. Type II — allows partial flux penetration (vortex state) between lower and upper critical fields. UPSC ANGLE: High-temperature superconductors, India's interest in Maglev technology. PYQ FREQUENCY: Meissner effect in UPSC GS-3 Science & Tech, IBPS PO GA, SSC CGL — 1× per 2 years.

questions.stem: The Hall effect in a current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field results in:

options.option_text: A transverse voltage (Hall voltage) perpendicular to both current and magnetic field — used to determine carrier type
An increase in resistance proportional to the square of the magnetic field strength applied
A change in temperature along the current direction due to magnetocaloric interaction (not this)
The expulsion of current carriers from the conductor's surface into the external circuit (not this)

questions.explanation: HALL EFFECT (1879, Edwin Hall): When current (I) flows through a conductor/semiconductor in a magnetic field (B perpendicular to I), charge carriers experience a LORENTZ FORCE sideways → accumulate on one face → create a HALL VOLTAGE (V_H) perpendicular to both I and B. V_H = IB/(ned) where n = carrier density, e = charge, d = thickness. USES: (1) Determine whether carriers are positive (p-type) or negative (n-type) — polarity of V_H tells us the sign of carriers. (2) Measure magnetic field strength (Hall sensors in smartphones, cars, industrial machines). (3) Measure carrier concentration (n). HALL COEFFICIENT R_H = V_H × d / (I × B) = 1/(ne) for electrons. SIGN: positive Hall coefficient → holes (p-type). Negative → electrons (n-type). OPTION B: magnetoresistance is a different effect (resistance changes with B field). UPSC ANGLE: Hall sensors used in EVs, wind turbines, BLDC motors — common in India's EV push. PYQ FREQUENCY: Hall effect definition and uses in CBSE XII, JEE, SSC CGL, IBPS PO Physics — 1× per 2-3 years.

questions.stem: Magnetic declination at a location on Earth is defined as the angle between:

options.option_text: Geographic north (true north) and magnetic north (compass direction) at that location
The direction of Earth's magnetic field and the horizontal plane at that location
The geographic equator and the magnetic equator measured along the meridian
The vertical component and the total intensity of Earth's magnetic field at that point

questions.explanation: MAGNETIC DECLINATION: the angle (measured in degrees E or W) between TRUE NORTH (geographic north, direction to the North Pole) and MAGNETIC NORTH (direction a compass needle points, toward the Magnetic North Pole). VARIATION: declination varies by location and changes slowly over time (secular variation, because Earth's molten outer core convection shifts the magnetic poles). EAST DECLINATION: magnetic north is east of true north (compass shows east of true north). WEST DECLINATION: compass shows west of true north. INDIA: declination ranges from ~0.5°W in Odisha to ~2°W in NW India (approximate). MAGNETIC DIP (option B): angle of Earth's field with the horizontal — a DIFFERENT element. MAGNETIC EQUATOR (option C): a different concept — the line of zero dip. NAVIGATION IMPORTANCE: sailors and pilots must correct for declination to navigate accurately. GPS has no such issue (it uses satellite geometry). PYQ FREQUENCY: magnetic declination definition in SSC CGL, IBPS PO Physics GA — 1× per cycle.
